_meta.purpose: Field-by-field legal/regulatory interpretation layer for the religion-vs-secular comparison tool. Consumed by the HTML as hover content, sidebar drawer, and inline explainer. Not a deliverable on its own.
_meta.scope: Covers every field in data/codebook.json plus comparison-pair and NTEE-subgroup framing.
_meta.rate_construction_in_use: Every per-filing rate in this file uses n_distinct_filings_with_at_least_one_row / n_canonical_filings (the disclose-rate construction). Conditional rates (in-default loans, unwritten loans, §512(b)(13) controlled, sentinel names) use a different denominator (rows in the relevant table) and are explicitly labeled.
_meta.year_range: All headline numbers are 2014-2024 (excl partial 2025). 2025 is a partial cohort — snapshot date 2026-05-24.
principles: Disclosure rate is not wrongdoing rate. High disclosure can mean more wrongdoing OR more conscientious reporting OR more complex related-party architecture.
Religion corpus is voluntary-filer subset under the church-exemption hole (IRC §6033(a)(3)(A)(i)). Secular corpus has no comparable hole. All ratios are filer-vs-filer.
No external fraud-label joins; the disclosure itself is the signal.

sched_l_excess_benefit.amt_tax_imposed.what_it_is: First-tier §4958 excise tax imposed on the disqualified person, equal to 25% of the excess benefit (Reg. §53.4958-1(c)).
sched_l_excess_benefit.amt_tax_imposed.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Reporting an amount here is a tax admission: the org has identified a transaction it concedes was excess and assessed the 25% tax. Filers do not volunteer these entries. In the religion corpus (2014-2024 excl partial-2025): 50 canonical filings disclosed at least one Pt I row, across 27 distinct EINs, totaling 84 raw rows — the disclosed floor, not the population. Secular corpus over the same period: 307 canonical filings at 203 EINs (446 raw rows). The Grassley 2011 staff memo treated any populated Pt I row as the strongest single Form 990 fraud indicator.
sched_l_excess_benefit.amt_tax_imposed.what_a_high_rate_means: A sector with elevated Pt I rates has either more bad behavior, more scrupulous compliance counsel forcing disclosure, or a higher base rate of IRS audit pressure pushing voluntary correction. Of the three, the second is the rarest — most CPAs advise against populating this box unless cornered.
sched_l_excess_benefit.amt_tax_imposed.what_a_low_rate_means: Either cleaner operations or, more likely, suppression: counsel writes the transaction up as ordinary compensation rather than as excess benefit, or the org never characterizes a benefit as 'excess' in the first place. A zero rate is consistent with both compliance and concealment.
sched_l_excess_benefit.amt_tax_imposed.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Under the disclose-rate construction [n distinct filings with ≥1 Pt I row / n canonical filings], religion §4958 rate is 0.0578% (50 of 86,455 filings flagged) against secular 0.0265% (307 of 1,160,678) — a 2.19× gap, 2014-2024. Two non-exclusive readings: (a) religious orgs disproportionately have founder-CEO structures that produce excess-benefit risk, or (b) the ECFA-member subset of religious filers is more likely to use voluntary correction as a fraud-management tool. Both are consistent with the data.
sched_l_excess_benefit.amt_tax_imposed.subgroup_caveats: Religion is NOT the leader. Of the 24 NTEE majors, Mental Health & Crisis (F) leads at 0.1112% (32 of 28,772 filings); religion (X) ranks #2 at 0.0578%; Medical Research (H) is #3 at 0.0445%. Sectors with single-founder structures (F, X) cluster high; sectors with bureaucratic governance (L Housing at 0.0052%, M Public Safety at 0.0088%) cluster near zero. Social Science (V) is the only major with zero disclosures.

sched_l_excess_benefit.amt_tax_reimburse.what_it_is: Excise tax the organization reimbursed back to the disqualified person.
sched_l_excess_benefit.amt_tax_reimburse.statutory_basis: Treas. Reg. §53.4958-7(d) — reimbursement of §4958 tax is itself a new excess benefit unless treated as compensation and pre-approved. https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/53.4958-7
sched_l_excess_benefit.amt_tax_reimburse.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Any non-zero entry here is a second, downstream excess-benefit transaction in the making. The reimbursement triggers the 200% second-tier tax if not itself corrected. Across the full Pt I corpus, n=1 with $13,000 reimbursed — vanishingly rare because counsel will not let a client populate this.
sched_l_excess_benefit.amt_tax_reimburse.what_a_high_rate_means: Extreme rarity. A non-zero entry typically signals an under-counseled filer who literally did the thing the regulation forbids.
sched_l_excess_benefit.amt_tax_reimburse.what_a_low_rate_means: Either compliance or, more often, that orgs that did reimburse simply mischaracterized the payment as W-2 compensation rather than disclosing it here.
sched_l_excess_benefit.amt_tax_reimburse.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Both corpora effectively zero. Not a usable comparison metric — use Pt I amt_tax_imposed instead.

sched_l_excess_benefit.transaction_corre.what_it_is: Was the excess benefit corrected within the §4958 correction period? Correction (full restitution to the org) eliminates the 200% second-tier tax under IRC §4958(b).
sched_l_excess_benefit.transaction_corre.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: transaction_corrected=False with a real Pt I entry is a live exposure: the org has admitted the excess benefit but not yet undone it, and the 200% tax clock is running. The full Pt I corpus shows zero uncorrected entries, which means filers who populate Pt I are also the ones who follow through on correction — consistent with these being the conscientious-disclosure subset.
sched_l_excess_benefit.transaction_corre.what_a_high_rate_means: A sector with many uncorrected entries would suggest disclosure-without-remediation — the worst signal. Doesn't actually appear in the data.
sched_l_excess_benefit.transaction_corre.what_a_low_rate_means: Either no excess benefits (most filings) or excess benefits that were corrected (most that were disclosed).
sched_l_excess_benefit.transaction_corre.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Correction-completion is a behavioral choice once disclosure happens. If the secular sector has uncorrected entries while religion does not, that itself is a finding about which filer type follows through.
sched_l_excess_benefit.transaction_corre.subgroup_caveats: Cell sizes are too small in most majors to compute correction rates.

sched_l_excess_benefit.relationship.what_it_is: Free-text description of the disqualified person's role: CEO, FOUNDER, BOARD CHAIR, FAMILY MEMBER, etc.
sched_l_excess_benefit.relationship.statutory_basis: IRC §4958(f)(1) defines 'disqualified person' as someone who, within the last five years, was in a position to exercise substantial influence over the affairs of the org. https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/4958
sched_l_excess_benefit.relationship.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: The relationship type tells you which governance failure produced the excess benefit. FOUNDER and CEO entries suggest unchecked-leader structures; FAMILY MEMBER and SUBSTANTIAL CONTRIBUTOR entries suggest the org has functionally become a personal vehicle for a single household or donor.
sched_l_excess_benefit.relationship.what_a_high_rate_means: Concentration of FOUNDER/CEO in this column across a sector flags founder-dominated governance — the structural precondition for excess-benefit risk under Reg. §53.4958-3.
sched_l_excess_benefit.relationship.what_a_low_rate_means: If relationships are diverse (varied job titles, no founder-cluster), excess benefits are likelier to be isolated incidents than systemic.
sched_l_excess_benefit.relationship.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis (not measured in this corpus): the regulatory literature predicts religion-corpus relationships skew toward FOUNDER/PASTOR/MINISTER labels and secular toward CEO/BOARD MEMBER/FAMILY MEMBER. Whether the actual disclosure text bears this out requires Pt I free-text analysis that has not been performed on this dataset.
sched_l_excess_benefit.relationship.subgroup_caveats: Too few rows to stratify cleanly by NTEE major.

sched_l_excess_benefit.description.what_it_is: Free-text description of the excess-benefit transaction itself — what the disqualified person actually received.
sched_l_excess_benefit.description.statutory_basis: Treas. Reg. §53.4958-4 defines what counts as 'excess benefit': economic benefit beyond consideration received by the org. https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/53.4958-4
sched_l_excess_benefit.description.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: The description text is the most diagnostic single field in the entire 990 dataset for understanding what insiders are doing. 'Personal use of credit card,' 'home renovation,' 'undocumented loan forgiven,' 'family member salary in excess of FMV' are the recurring patterns named in IRS guidance and the Grassley inquiry. Free-text mining of this column across both corpora is a high-yield future task.
sched_l_excess_benefit.description.what_a_high_rate_means: Not applicable as a rate — read by content, not frequency.
sched_l_excess_benefit.description.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis (not measured in this corpus): regulatory and journalistic literature on prosperity ministries predicts religion descriptions tilt toward housing-allowance overage and ministry-expense personal-use; secular tilts toward vendor-kickback and inflated-salary patterns. Free-text analysis of Pt I description has not been performed on this dataset; the statute treats both identically.
sched_l_excess_benefit.description.subgroup_caveats: Read at the field level, not the sector level.

sched_l_loans.original_principal.what_it_is: Original principal of an insider loan, in dollars.
sched_l_loans.original_principal.statutory_basis: Reportable under Form 990 Schedule L Pt II per Reg. §1.6033-2(a)(2)(ii)(I); fairness/market terms governed by Reg. §53.4958-4(b).
sched_l_loans.original_principal.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Round-number principals ($50k, $100k, $250k) without amortization schedules are an ECFA-flagged pattern — the Grassley inquiry found multiple six- and seven-figure round-number loans to officers at the prosperity ministries. The dollar amount alone is necessary but not sufficient; pair with written_agreement and in_default to read meaning.
sched_l_loans.original_principal.what_a_high_rate_means: Sectors with high median principals (Education, Health Care) often reflect legitimate housing-loan programs for recruited faculty or physicians; sectors with high principals AND high unwritten-loan rates flag insider extraction.
sched_l_loans.original_principal.what_a_low_rate_means: Small principals or many zeros usually mean petty insider advances and travel-expense floats — lower risk per loan but easier to normalize into ongoing extraction.
sched_l_loans.original_principal.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Per-filing insider-loan disclosure rates are close: religion 4.70% (4,066 of 86,455 filings) ranks #2 of 24 majors; Arts (A) leads at 4.89%. Per-loan principal-size distribution is not aggregated in current rel_vs_sec.json — claim about religion-vs-secular median principal magnitudes requires a numeric run not present in this revision's data inputs.
sched_l_loans.original_principal.subgroup_caveats: Education and Health Care have high principals for non-fraud reasons (recruitment loans); read alongside written_agreement and approved_by_board.

sched_l_loans.balance_due.what_it_is: Balance due at the end of the tax period. Negative values indicate a credit/refund position in the relationship.
sched_l_loans.balance_due.statutory_basis: Same as original_principal; the balance vs. principal ratio approximates loan-amortization adherence.
sched_l_loans.balance_due.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Balance ≥ original principal multiple years running implies the loan is interest-only or unpaid — economically equivalent to an indefinite advance. If the loan is later forgiven, the entire balance becomes an excess-benefit transaction under Reg. §53.4958-4(a)(1).
sched_l_loans.balance_due.what_a_high_rate_means: Persistent balance-due across years (read as time series, not single year) flags evergreen insider lending. Single-year snapshots aren't enough.
sched_l_loans.balance_due.what_a_low_rate_means: Declining balance against original principal is the boring, healthy signal: amortization is happening.
sched_l_loans.balance_due.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Compute balance_due / original_principal at the loan level; sectors with persistent ratios near 1.0 are the watch list. Per-loan ratio not aggregated in current rel_vs_sec.json.
sched_l_loans.balance_due.subgroup_caveats: Some sectors (Housing & Shelter, Community Improvement) carry deliberately long-term low-interest insider loans for legitimate program reasons; check loan_to_organization direction and purpose_of_loan text.

sched_l_loans.loan_to_organization.what_it_is: True = the insider lent money TO the org (the org owes the insider).
sched_l_loans.loan_to_organization.statutory_basis: Reg. §53.4958-4(b)(2)(ii)(B) treats below-market loans from insiders as potential excess benefit running the opposite direction.
sched_l_loans.loan_to_organization.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Loans from insiders to the org are not usually the dangerous direction — the insider is taking risk, not extracting value. But they can mask: (1) above-market interest paid to the insider, (2) pension substitutes for a founder taking 'loan repayment' as deferred comp, (3) collateral pledges that effectively put org assets behind insider personal lending.
sched_l_loans.loan_to_organization.what_a_high_rate_means: High loan_to_organization share is common in young or financially fragile orgs where the founder is bankrolling operations. Not inherently a fraud signal; cross-check with comp from related orgs and severance.
sched_l_loans.loan_to_organization.what_a_low_rate_means: Most insider loans run the other direction — the org lending to the insider, which is the riskier vector.
sched_l_loans.loan_to_organization.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis (not measured in this corpus): regulatory framing predicts religion has a higher share of insider-to-org loans (founder-bankrolled startups) and secular a higher share of org-to-insider. The split has not been quantified in current data files.
sched_l_loans.loan_to_organization.subgroup_caveats: Arts & Culture (A) and religion are nearly tied on overall insider-loan rate; direction-split has not been computed here.

sched_l_loans.loan_from_organization.what_it_is: True = the org lent money TO the insider. The higher-risk direction.
sched_l_loans.loan_from_organization.statutory_basis: Reg. §53.4958-4(a) — below-market or undocumented org-to-insider loans are presumptively excess-benefit transactions absent the rebuttable-presumption procedure under Reg. §53.4958-6.
sched_l_loans.loan_from_organization.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Org-to-insider loans are the canonical §4958 risk vector. If terms are below-market, the difference is excess benefit. If unwritten or unapproved, the rebuttable presumption is unavailable and the IRS may treat the entire amount as excess benefit. The Grassley inquiry traced multiple seven-figure unrepaid org-to-officer loans at three of the six investigated ministries.
sched_l_loans.loan_from_organization.what_a_high_rate_means: Concentrated org-to-insider lending in a sector flags insider-extraction architecture. The most diagnostic version is paired with unwritten + unapproved + in_default.
sched_l_loans.loan_from_organization.what_a_low_rate_means: Most orgs do not lend to insiders. A near-zero rate is the norm and the safe baseline.
sched_l_loans.loan_from_organization.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Both corpora populate Sched L Pt II at similar rates overall (religion 4.70%, several secular majors in the 3-5% band); the diagnostic signal lies in the boolean co-grid of org-direction + unwritten + unapproved, which is not currently computed at the religion-vs-secular level.
sched_l_loans.loan_from_organization.subgroup_caveats: Education (B) carries large absolute counts of insider loans because of faculty/admin housing programs; rate it against written_agreement and approved_by_board before interpreting.

sched_l_loans.written_agreement.what_it_is: True = the loan terms are in a written agreement.
sched_l_loans.written_agreement.statutory_basis: ECFA Standard 6 explicitly requires written agreements; Reg. §53.4958-6(c) makes contemporaneous documentation a prerequisite for the rebuttable presumption of reasonableness.
sched_l_loans.written_agreement.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: An unwritten insider loan is the single Grassley-named pattern most associated with prosperity-ministry abuse. Without written terms there is no rebuttable presumption; without rebuttable presumption the IRS sets the FMV baseline; without an FMV baseline almost any loan is exposed as excess benefit.
sched_l_loans.written_agreement.what_a_high_rate_means: Conditional rate (denominator = loan rows with written_agreement non-null): religion unwritten share 39.9% (2,446 of 6,123 loan rows), secular 31.8% (18,661 of 58,634). Religion is 1.26× the secular unwritten rate. Systemic documentation failure on both sides.
sched_l_loans.written_agreement.what_a_low_rate_means: High written-agreement rates indicate professionalized board governance; correlate with ECFA membership and Single Audit obligations in the religion corpus.
sched_l_loans.written_agreement.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Religion 1.26× secular unwritten rate (39.9% vs 31.8%, conditional on loan rows with non-null written_agreement; n=6,123 religion loan rows vs n=58,634 secular). Consistent with smaller, less-professionalized board structures and less in-house counsel — the church-status filers are smaller orgs on average.
sched_l_loans.written_agreement.subgroup_caveats: Smaller orgs (lower NTEE-major median revenue) systematically have higher unwritten rates regardless of religion classification — control for org size before reading this as a religion-specific finding. The full unwritten×unapproved cogrid has not been recomputed in this revision.

sched_l_loans.in_default.what_it_is: True = the insider loan is in default at year-end.
sched_l_loans.in_default.statutory_basis: Reg. §53.4958-4(a)(1)(i) — a forgiven insider loan is treated as excess benefit equal to the unpaid balance.
sched_l_loans.in_default.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: A defaulted insider loan that the org subsequently forgives is a textbook excess-benefit transaction. The IRS treats forgiveness as the equivalent of cash compensation, with no FMV defense available because no service was rendered for the forgiven balance.
sched_l_loans.in_default.what_a_high_rate_means: Even a small absolute rate is concerning because defaulted loans are the leading edge of forgiveness-as-comp.
sched_l_loans.in_default.what_a_low_rate_means: Low default rate is the norm; absence of default doesn't preclude below-market terms or interest-only loans.
sched_l_loans.in_default.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Conditional rate (denominator = loan rows with in_default non-null): religion 0.67% (41 of 6,150 loan rows), secular 0.77% (452 of 58,873). Ratio 0.87× — religion is slightly LOWER. One of the few comparison metrics where religion shows no elevated rate; default-and-forgive appears sector-agnostic.
sched_l_loans.in_default.subgroup_caveats: Sectors with very small loan populations show statistical noise in this metric — require n_loans ≥ ~200 to compute a stable rate.

sched_l_loans.approved_by_board.what_it_is: True = the loan was approved by the board or a board-authorized committee.
sched_l_loans.approved_by_board.statutory_basis: Reg. §53.4958-6(a)(1) — board approval by independent persons is one of three prerequisites for the rebuttable presumption of reasonableness.
sched_l_loans.approved_by_board.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: An unapproved insider loan defeats the rebuttable presumption, which means in any §4958 challenge the IRS — not the org — sets the FMV baseline. The Grassley inquiry found multiple cases where six-figure officer loans were arranged unilaterally by the CEO without board approval.
sched_l_loans.approved_by_board.what_a_high_rate_means: Approved-rate near 100% is the healthy signal; below ~85% flags weak board oversight of insider transactions.
sched_l_loans.approved_by_board.what_a_low_rate_means: Unapproved insider loans = unilateral CEO action = the structural precondition for §4958 exposure.
sched_l_loans.approved_by_board.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: regulatory framing predicts religion has a higher unapproved-loan rate than secular, concentrated in church-status filers with smaller, founder-dominated boards. The conditional approved-rate by sector has not been recomputed in current rel_vs_sec.json (the unwritten rate is the closest available proxy).
sched_l_loans.approved_by_board.subgroup_caveats: Sectors with controlled-by-parent governance (Health Care system subsidiaries) may show low approval rates not because of insider extraction but because parent-board approval substitutes for subsidiary-board approval — a structural artifact, not a fraud signal.

sched_l_loans.relationship.what_it_is: Free-text description of the borrower's relationship to the org.
sched_l_loans.relationship.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: OFFICER and FOUNDER labels are the highest-risk; FAMILY MEMBER is the second-degree pattern. Sentinel labels (INTERESTED PERSON, RELATED PARTY) defeat downstream identification.
sched_l_loans.relationship.what_a_high_rate_means: Concentration of FAMILY MEMBER and SPOUSE in this field signals the org has become a household vehicle.
sched_l_loans.relationship.what_a_low_rate_means: Diverse relationship vocabulary suggests transactional loans rather than systemic insider lending.
sched_l_loans.relationship.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis (not measured in this corpus): the relationship-label distribution between corpora has not been tabulated; the sentinel-name conditional rate is religion 6.1% vs secular 9.3% (religion uses fewer placeholder labels), but the substantive label distribution behind that is not in current data files.
sched_l_loans.relationship.subgroup_caveats: Sentinel-strip first; never trust raw distinct-count from this field.

sched_l_loans.purpose_of_loan.statutory_basis: No direct statutory standard — read for content.
sched_l_loans.purpose_of_loan.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: 'Housing,' 'relocation,' 'startup capital' are the legitimate purposes per ECFA guidance and IRS audit history; 'personal,' 'travel,' 'unspecified,' or blank are the watch-list purposes. 'Working capital advance' in a recurring loan is regulatorily a synonym for pension substitute.
sched_l_loans.purpose_of_loan.what_a_high_rate_means: Not rate-based; read free text by content.
sched_l_loans.purpose_of_loan.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: regulatory and ministry-finance literature predicts religion purpose-text leans toward parsonage-and-mission-trip vocabulary while secular leans toward working-capital-and-bridge vocabulary. No purpose-text analysis has been run on this corpus.

sched_l_grants_to_interested.amount_of_a.what_it_is: Dollar amount of a grant or assistance benefiting an officer/director/trustee/key employee or family member.
sched_l_grants_to_interested.amount_of_a.statutory_basis: Form 990 Schedule L Pt III; Reg. §1.6033-2(a)(2)(ii)(I); excess-benefit analysis under Reg. §53.4958-4.
sched_l_grants_to_interested.amount_of_a.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: PLR 200437040 treated an improperly directed scholarship to an insider's child as an excess benefit. Where the grant lacks an objective selection process, the entire amount can be characterized as compensation — and if not on the W-2, as excess benefit. The dollar amount itself flags whether the diversion is symbolic ($500 to a board kid) or substantive ($25,000 to the founder's spouse).
sched_l_grants_to_interested.amount_of_a.what_a_high_rate_means: Concentrated large-dollar Pt III grants in a sector flag scholarship-as-conduit patterns.
sched_l_grants_to_interested.amount_of_a.what_a_low_rate_means: Low rates suggest either compliant scholarship programs with objective criteria, or absence of formal grant-making.
sched_l_grants_to_interested.amount_of_a.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Per-filing Pt III rates and grant-amount distributions are not in current rel_vs_sec.json or subgroup_with_religion.json. Sector-level comparison is not numerically grounded in this revision.
sched_l_grants_to_interested.amount_of_a.subgroup_caveats: Education (B) and Philanthropy (T) have legitimate high-grant volumes that aren't insider-directed; rate is misleading without joining to relationship field.

sched_l_grants_to_interested.relationshi.what_it_is: How the grant recipient is related to the org.
sched_l_grants_to_interested.relationshi.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: FAMILY MEMBER is the canonical signal — the scholarship-to-founder's-child or housing-to-founder's-parent pattern. SUBSTANTIAL CONTRIBUTOR is the second — the donor-as-grantee circular flow.
sched_l_grants_to_interested.relationshi.what_a_high_rate_means: Sectors with high FAMILY MEMBER share in this field are the watch list.
sched_l_grants_to_interested.relationshi.what_a_low_rate_means: OFFICER-self grants are usually relocation/housing benefits captured separately on Sched J; presence here without Sched J reciprocity is suspicious.
sched_l_grants_to_interested.relationshi.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: regulatory framing predicts religion has a higher FAMILY MEMBER / SPOUSE share and secular a higher OFFICER / DIRECTOR share. Pt III relationship distribution has not been tabulated in current data.

sched_l_grants_to_interested.type_of_ass.what_it_is: Form of assistance: scholarship, housing, medical, etc.
sched_l_grants_to_interested.type_of_ass.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: 'Housing' is the dual signal: legitimate parsonage under §107 OR insider housing benefit. 'Scholarship' to a family member is the PLR 200437040 pattern. 'Medical' to a founder is rare and almost always excess benefit.
sched_l_grants_to_interested.type_of_ass.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: the §107 housing exclusion makes 'housing' over-represented in religion Pt III relative to secular; tuition is common to both. Type-of-assistance distribution has not been tabulated in current data.
sched_l_grants_to_interested.type_of_ass.subgroup_caveats: Education (B) has high tuition-grant volume that is mostly compliant; flag only when paired with FAMILY MEMBER relationship.

sched_l_business_transactions.transactio.what_it_is: Aggregate dollar amount of business transactions with this interested person during the tax year. The $100k aggregate-per-person threshold triggers required disclosure.
sched_l_business_transactions.transactio.statutory_basis: Form 990 Schedule L Pt IV; Reg. §1.6033-2(a)(2)(ii)(I). FMV/reasonableness governed by Reg. §53.4958-4(b).
sched_l_business_transactions.transactio.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Pt IV is the most diagnostically rich Schedule L part because the disclosure rule is mandatory (≥$100k aggregate) rather than self-incriminating. The Grassley inquiry traced 'founder's-spouse-as-vendor,' 'board-member's-construction-company,' and 'related-LLC-as-landlord' patterns through this field. The dollar amount alone doesn't establish wrongdoing — fair-market-value paid to a related vendor is legal — but it sets the bound for any §4958 excess-benefit analysis.
sched_l_business_transactions.transactio.what_a_high_rate_means: Sectors with high Pt IV disclosure rates (Health Care 11.38%, Science & Tech 9.10%, Medical Research 8.70%) reflect structural use of related-vendor relationships, not necessarily insider extraction. The signal sharpens when paired with sharing_of_revenues=True or FAMILY MEMBER relationship.
sched_l_business_transactions.transactio.what_a_low_rate_means: Low disclosure rate may mean (a) genuinely arm's-length sourcing, or (b) sub-threshold transactions structured to stay below $100k.
sched_l_business_transactions.transactio.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Per-filing rate: religion Pt IV 4.83% (4,173 of 86,455 filings) ranks #19 of 24 majors — well below the secular median. Range across secular sectors: 2.29% (Public Safety, M) to 11.38% (Health Care, E). Religion is below most secular sectors — partly because religious orgs are smaller and cross the $100k threshold less often.
sched_l_business_transactions.transactio.subgroup_caveats: Health Care (E) leads at 11.38% because of physician-owned-practice and physician-supplier relationships that are sector-structural, not fraud. Religion sits among the lowest because smaller orgs cross the $100k threshold less often.

sched_l_business_transactions.relationsh.what_it_is: How the counterparty is related to the org: family member, business affiliate, substantial contributor, etc.
sched_l_business_transactions.relationsh.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: FAMILY MEMBER and SUBSTANTIAL CONTRIBUTOR are the highest-risk labels. Family-member-as-vendor is the canonical Grassley pattern; substantial-contributor-as-vendor is the donor-conduit pattern that converts charitable contributions into vendor revenue back to the donor.
sched_l_business_transactions.relationsh.what_a_high_rate_means: Concentration of FAMILY MEMBER in Pt IV is the strongest in-dataset signal of household-as-org architecture.
sched_l_business_transactions.relationsh.what_a_low_rate_means: OFFICER-self vendor relationships are common and usually involve owned consulting LLCs; less inherently risky than family-member vendor relationships.
sched_l_business_transactions.relationsh.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: regulatory framing predicts religion's Pt IV relationship labels skew toward FAMILY MEMBER and secular toward BUSINESS AFFILIATE. Pt IV relationship distribution has not been tabulated in current data.

sched_l_business_transactions.descriptio.what_it_is: Free-text description of the business transaction.
sched_l_business_transactions.descriptio.statutory_basis: No direct statutory standard — read by content.
sched_l_business_transactions.descriptio.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: This is the single highest-yield free-text field in the corpus. 'Consulting services,' 'rent paid to' (followed by an owned-LLC name), 'construction services,' 'marketing services' are the recurring vendor archetypes named in IRS audit history. Vague descriptions ('professional services,' 'management fees') without further detail are red flags.
sched_l_business_transactions.descriptio.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis (not measured in this corpus): regulatory and ministry-finance literature predicts religion descriptions tilt toward rent/broadcasting/royalty/speaking-fee vocabulary; secular toward consulting/construction/IT/legal. Pt IV description text has not been mined for this dataset; the statutory FMV question is identical.

sched_l_business_transactions.sharing_of.what_it_is: True = the org and the interested person split revenues from the transaction.
sched_l_business_transactions.sharing_of.statutory_basis: Revenue-sharing with an insider is presumptive private inurement under Reg. §1.501(c)(3)-1(c)(2) and can be the precondition for an excess-benefit determination.
sched_l_business_transactions.sharing_of.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Revenue-sharing arrangements with insiders are among the most aggressive forms of related-party transaction because they create ongoing aligned interest between the org and a private party. The IRS historical position (cf. Rev. Rul. 69-383, GCM 39862) has been that revenue-sharing is permissible only with strict procedural safeguards, otherwise it is private inurement.
sched_l_business_transactions.sharing_of.what_a_high_rate_means: Even a small share is meaningful; this is a low-base-rate field where positives are diagnostic.
sched_l_business_transactions.sharing_of.what_a_low_rate_means: Most Pt IV transactions are flat-fee or per-unit; revenue-sharing is the exception.
sched_l_business_transactions.sharing_of.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Religion-vs-secular revenue-sharing rate is not separately tabulated in rel_vs_sec.json. Regulatory framing predicts religion may show concentrated revenue-sharing in media-and-broadcasting royalty contexts; numeric confirmation requires a metric not in current data.
sched_l_business_transactions.sharing_of.subgroup_caveats: Health Care (E) has some revenue-sharing in physician-services contexts that have specific carve-outs under Stark Law / Anti-Kickback Statute interaction with §4958; don't read pure rate without sector context.

sched_r_disregarded.total_income.what_it_is: Total income reported by a disregarded entity (typically a single-member LLC owned by the filer).
sched_r_disregarded.total_income.statutory_basis: Treas. Reg. §301.7701-3 — disregarded entity rules; its income flows through to the filer.
sched_r_disregarded.total_income.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Disregarded entities are usually legitimate (real-estate-holding LLC, programmatic subsidiary). The fraud-adjacent pattern is using a disregarded entity to hold property whose use benefits an insider, or to channel revenue away from the consolidating 990 in ways that obscure the source.
sched_r_disregarded.total_income.what_a_high_rate_means: High total_income in disregarded entities relative to filer total revenue indicates the org's real economic activity is happening below the parent-990 line.
sched_r_disregarded.total_income.what_a_low_rate_means: Low income / disregarded-as-shell-only is the more typical pattern; less analytically interesting.
sched_r_disregarded.total_income.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: regulatory framing predicts religion uses disregarded entities more for property-holding (parsonage, church real estate) and secular more for program subsidiaries. Disregarded-entity income distribution by sector has not been tabulated in current data.
sched_r_disregarded.total_income.subgroup_caveats: Housing & Shelter (L), Health Care (E) have legitimate program reasons for high-income disregarded entities; don't read in isolation.

sched_r_disregarded.end_of_year_assets.what_it_is: End-of-year assets held by the disregarded entity.
sched_r_disregarded.end_of_year_assets.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Assets parked in disregarded entities for ostensibly programmatic reasons can be the holding pattern for later transfers to related parties — the Catholic diocese cemetery-trust pattern that preceded multiple bankruptcies.
sched_r_disregarded.end_of_year_assets.what_a_high_rate_means: Disregarded entities holding most of the filer's real estate is the structural precondition for the pre-bankruptcy transfer pattern. Read with caution; not all such structures are predatory.
sched_r_disregarded.end_of_year_assets.what_a_low_rate_means: Most filers have small disregarded entities.
sched_r_disregarded.end_of_year_assets.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Asset-distribution by sector is not in current rel_vs_sec.json. Regulatory framing predicts religion may concentrate asset-holding in disregarded entities (real estate, broadcasting equipment) more than most secular sectors; not numerically confirmed here.
sched_r_disregarded.end_of_year_assets.subgroup_caveats: Housing & Shelter (L) by definition holds most assets in property-holding entities.

sched_r_disregarded.legal_domicile.what_it_is: US state or foreign country where the disregarded entity is legally domiciled.
sched_r_disregarded.legal_domicile.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Foreign domiciles (Cayman, BVI, Bermuda) for disregarded entities of US 501(c)(3) filers are rare and meaningful when they appear. Delaware/Nevada domicile is normal for asset-holding LLCs; specific tax-haven jurisdictions are not.
sched_r_disregarded.legal_domicile.what_a_high_rate_means: Sector-level offshore concentration is essentially absent in religious nonprofits; if it appears, investigate.
sched_r_disregarded.legal_domicile.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: International (Q) and Health Care (E) secular orgs have higher rates of foreign-domiciled disregarded entities for legitimate program reasons; religion is predicted to be overwhelmingly domestic. Sector-level domicile distribution has not been tabulated here.
sched_r_disregarded.legal_domicile.subgroup_caveats: International, Foreign Affairs (Q) is the obvious exception.

sched_r_disregarded.primary_activity.what_it_is: Free-text description of what the disregarded entity does.
sched_r_disregarded.primary_activity.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: 'Hold property,' 'real estate,' 'broadcasting' are common and usually benign. 'Investment activities,' 'consulting,' 'management services' to the parent are the patterns worth reading carefully.
sched_r_disregarded.primary_activity.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: regulatory framing predicts both corpora concentrate in 'real estate,' with religion adding 'broadcasting' / 'ministry' and secular adding 'program operations.' Primary-activity text has not been mined here.

sched_r_related_tax_exempt.legal_domicil.what_it_is: US state or foreign country where the related tax-exempt entity is domiciled.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.legal_domicil.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Most related tax-exempts share state with the filer. Foreign-domiciled affiliates are common only in International (Q) and a subset of religious mission organizations. Multi-state domicile patterns map denominational/system structure.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.legal_domicil.what_a_high_rate_means: Wide cross-state distribution among related entities typically reflects denominational or multi-state health-system structure — legitimate and informative, not fraud-adjacent.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.legal_domicil.what_a_low_rate_means: Same-state-only suggests a tightly localized affiliate group.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.legal_domicil.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: regulatory framing predicts religion has heavier cross-state domicile dispersion (denominational kin) and secular heavier in-state clustering (system-affiliated). Domicile distribution has not been tabulated in current data.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.legal_domicil.subgroup_caveats: International (Q) and large Health Care (E) systems are the multi-state exceptions.

sched_r_related_tax_exempt.exempt_code_s.what_it_is: IRC subsection under which the related entity is exempt: 501(c)(3), 501(c)(4), 501(c)(2), 527, etc.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.exempt_code_s.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: 501(c)(2) related entities are title-holding corps — the canonical real-estate-holding affiliate structure. 501(c)(4) related entities are the action-arm pattern (the 501(c)(3) does charity; the (c)(4) does advocacy). 527 related entities indicate the org has an associated PAC. Mixed (c)(3)/(c)(4)/527 family structures are not inherently improper but require careful funds-segregation analysis to avoid §501(c)(3) lobbying-limit violations.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.exempt_code_s.what_a_high_rate_means: Sectors with high (c)(4)+(c)(3) co-presence are advocacy-adjacent; sectors with high (c)(2) co-presence are real-estate-heavy.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.exempt_code_s.what_a_low_rate_means: Single-entity structures suggest simpler organizational architecture and lower transaction-laundering risk.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.exempt_code_s.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: regulatory framing predicts religion-corpus related entities skew toward (c)(2) (parsonage / property-holding) and secular toward (c)(4) and 527 (advocacy/political). Exempt-code distribution has not been tabulated here.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.exempt_code_s.subgroup_caveats: Civil Rights (R) and Community Improvement (S) have legitimately high (c)(4)/527 co-presence.

sched_r_related_tax_exempt.public_charit.what_it_is: Schedule A Part I line-code for the related entity's public-charity classification.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.public_charit.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: 509(a)(3) supporting-org affiliates (Type I/II/III, especially Type III non-functionally-integrated) are the regulatorily fraught structure. Type III SOs received tightened oversight after the Pension Protection Act of 2006 because of pre-2006 abuse patterns. Catholic-church-status affiliates often appear here too.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.public_charit.what_a_high_rate_means: High 509(a)(3) share in related-entity columns flags supporting-org architecture; cross-reference with section_512b_13_controlled.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.public_charit.what_a_low_rate_means: All-509(a)(1)/(2) related-entity profiles are simpler and lower-risk.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.public_charit.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: regulatory framing predicts religion concentrates in 170(b)(1)(A)(i) church-affiliate co-presence and secular in 509(a)(1) and 509(a)(3) co-presence. Public-charity status distribution has not been tabulated here.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.public_charit.subgroup_caveats: Philanthropy (T) has legitimately high 509(a)(3) presence; Health Care (E) has heavy 509(a)(1) hospital-affiliate presence.

sched_r_related_tax_exempt.section_512b_.what_it_is: True = the related entity is a 'controlled organization' under IRC §512(b)(13).
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.section_512b_.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Controlled-entity status triggers UBIT on interest, rent, royalty, and annuity payments from the controlled entity to the parent. The fraud-adjacent pattern is using control-relationships to move assets between affiliates pre-bankruptcy (multiple Catholic diocese cases: Milwaukee, Davenport, Tucson) or to route deductible donations through controlled fundraising entities back to operating affiliates.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.section_512b_.what_a_high_rate_means: High control rate indicates highly integrated corporate-family structures. Health Care systems and Housing systems naturally show high control rates because of system governance.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.section_512b_.what_a_low_rate_means: Low control rate suggests looser affiliate relationships — historically more typical for religious-denominational kinship.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.section_512b_.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Conditional rate (denominator = related-entity rows where section_512b_13_controlled is non-null): religion 31.2% (12,909 of 41,363 related-entity rows), secular 39.3% (1,115,388 of 2,840,235). Secular is 1.26× religion. Counter-intuitive only until you note that secular corpus is dominated by health-system and housing-system affiliates with formal control structures; religion corpus is dominated by denominational kin without formal control.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.section_512b_.subgroup_caveats: Per-filing (not conditional) Sched R Pt II disclosure rates by major: Housing & Shelter (L) leads at 52.18%, Health Care (E) 48.60%, Employment (J) 31.07%, Philanthropy (T) 29.03%, Community Improvement (S) 23.40%. Religion at 9.27% ranks #19 of 24 majors — well below the secular median by this measure.

sched_r_related_tax_exempt.primary_activ.what_it_is: Free-text description of what the related tax-exempt does.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.primary_activ.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Read by content. 'Hold property,' 'real estate,' 'foundation' are common. 'Fundraising' as a related entity's sole activity, with most cash flowing back to the parent, can be the donor-conduit pattern.
sched_r_related_tax_exempt.primary_activ.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis (not measured in this corpus): regulatory framing predicts religion-corpus related-entity activity skews toward church/ministry/broadcasting/mission descriptors, secular toward foundation/fundraising/real estate/operating descriptors. No related-activity text mining in current data.

sched_r_related_partnership.percentage_o.what_it_is: Filer's percentage ownership in the related partnership.
sched_r_related_partnership.percentage_o.statutory_basis: IRC §704 partnership taxation; UBIT analysis under §512(c) for partnership-source income.
sched_r_related_partnership.percentage_o.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: High ownership in for-profit partnerships subjects the filer to UBIT on partnership income that doesn't qualify as substantially related. The fraud-adjacent pattern is using partnership structure to route insider compensation as 'guaranteed payments' or 'distributions' instead of as W-2 comp.
sched_r_related_partnership.percentage_o.what_a_high_rate_means: Concentrated high-ownership partnership stakes indicate the filer is operating substantial commercial activity through partnership form.
sched_r_related_partnership.percentage_o.what_a_low_rate_means: Low or zero ownership suggests passive investor partnerships, lower UBIT exposure, less insider-comp risk.
sched_r_related_partnership.percentage_o.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: secular sectors (Education, Health Care) likely carry higher partnership-ownership patterns than religion based on regulatory framing of endowment-investment and physician-practice partnerships. Partnership-ownership distribution by sector has not been tabulated here.
sched_r_related_partnership.percentage_o.subgroup_caveats: Education (B) endowment-investment partnerships, Health Care (E) physician-practice partnerships are sector-structural.

sched_r_related_partnership.share_total_.what_it_is: Filer's share of the related partnership's total income.
sched_r_related_partnership.share_total_.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Empty across the corpus in current data. Where populated in source data, would diagnose the UBIT magnitude of partnership income; absence in parsed data means this analytical axis is unavailable for both corpora.

sched_r_related_partnership.share_end_of.what_it_is: Filer's share of the partnership's end-of-year assets.
sched_r_related_partnership.share_end_of.statutory_basis: Partnership asset allocation; aggregate UBIT context.

sched_r_related_partnership.general_or_m.what_it_is: True = the filer is a general or managing partner.
sched_r_related_partnership.general_or_m.statutory_basis: Partnership management role determines UBIT treatment under §512(c) and operational control attribution.
sched_r_related_partnership.general_or_m.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: GP/managing partner status means the filer controls operations — raising UBIT exposure and making partnership activities attributable to the filer for inurement analysis. Limited-partner roles are more passive and lower risk.
sched_r_related_partnership.general_or_m.what_a_high_rate_means: High GP rate indicates active operational use of partnership form.
sched_r_related_partnership.general_or_m.what_a_low_rate_means: Mostly limited-partner profiles indicate investment-only partnership use.
sched_r_related_partnership.general_or_m.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: regulatory framing predicts religion participates as limited-partner where it participates at all, while secular Education and Health Care take substantial GP/managing roles. GP-vs-LP split by sector has not been tabulated here.
sched_r_related_partnership.general_or_m.subgroup_caveats: Sector-structural; not a fraud signal on its own.

sched_r_related_partnership.disprortion_.what_it_is: True = the partnership uses a disproportionate income allocation under §704(b) that diverges from capital contributions.
sched_r_related_partnership.disprortion_.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Disproportionate allocations are legitimate when they have substantial economic effect; abusive when they route income/loss to tax-exempt partners to shield income from UBIT. Empty in current corpus.

sched_r_related_partnership.primary_pred.what_it_is: Free-text description of the partnership's main income type.
sched_r_related_partnership.primary_pred.statutory_basis: Maps to UBIT analysis: rental income (§512(b)(3)), royalties (§512(b)(2)), debt-financed (§514).

sched_r_related_partnership.legal_domici.what_it_is: US state or foreign country of the partnership.
sched_r_related_partnership.legal_domici.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Foreign-domiciled related partnerships are rare and meaningful when they appear at non-International filers.
sched_r_related_partnership.legal_domici.what_a_high_rate_means: Concentrated offshore partnership domicile is essentially absent in religion; uncommon but present in some Health Care and International secular filers.
sched_r_related_partnership.legal_domici.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: religion is overwhelmingly domestic; secular has narrow offshore exposure in specific sectors (International Q, some Health Care). Partnership-domicile distribution by sector has not been tabulated here.

sched_r_related_corp_trust.percentage_ow.what_it_is: Filer's percentage ownership of the related corporation or trust.
sched_r_related_corp_trust.percentage_ow.statutory_basis: IRC §512(b)(13) control test uses 50%+ voting power for corp control; 80%+ value for trust control.
sched_r_related_corp_trust.percentage_ow.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: 100% ownership of a C-corp typically means the filer has a taxable-corp subsidiary used to run UBIT-likely activities. The fraud-adjacent question is whether intercompany transfers (rent, royalty, dividend, interest) are at arm's length — the §482 question applied to a tax-exempt context.
sched_r_related_corp_trust.percentage_ow.what_a_high_rate_means: Wholly-owned taxable subsidiaries are normal in Health Care and Education; less common in religion.
sched_r_related_corp_trust.percentage_ow.what_a_low_rate_means: Minority interests are more passive, less fraud-adjacent.
sched_r_related_corp_trust.percentage_ow.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: secular sectors carry systematically higher percentage_ownership values in related corp/trust columns than religion based on sector-structural reasons. Ownership distribution by sector has not been tabulated here.
sched_r_related_corp_trust.percentage_ow.subgroup_caveats: Health Care (E) and Education (B) lead for sector-structural reasons.

sched_r_related_corp_trust.share_total_i.what_it_is: Filer's share of related corp/trust total income.
sched_r_related_corp_trust.share_total_i.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Empty in current corpus; analytical axis unavailable.

sched_r_related_corp_trust.share_end_of_.what_it_is: Filer's share of related corp/trust end-of-year assets.

sched_r_related_corp_trust.type_of_entit.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: C-corp subsidiaries of 501(c)(3)s are typically used to insulate UBIT-prone activities; trust subsidiaries (especially supporting-org-type 509(a)(3) trusts) are the more common structure for endowment-segregated activities. Excessive use of trust form for fee-generating activities can indicate income-shielding architecture.
sched_r_related_corp_trust.type_of_entit.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: regulatory framing predicts religion may carry more trust subsidiaries (endowment, parsonage-trust, denominational pension trusts) and secular more C-corp subsidiaries (taxable activity insulation). Entity-type distribution by sector has not been tabulated here.

sched_r_related_corp_trust.section_512b_.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Same as the tax-exempt counterpart — controlled status triggers UBIT on interest/rent/royalty/annuity from sub to parent. Where the controlled entity is a for-profit subsidiary, control-rate ≈ 100% is normal; what matters is whether intercompany pricing is arm's-length.
sched_r_related_corp_trust.section_512b_.what_a_high_rate_means: High control rate in for-profit related entities is structural; in tax-exempt related entities it's the integration signal.
sched_r_related_corp_trust.section_512b_.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Same combined-conditional pattern as the tax-exempt counterpart: religion 31.2%, secular 39.3% under the combined related-tax-exempt + related-corp-trust denominator. Religion is below the secular average; the gap reflects formal system architecture density in secular Health Care and Housing rather than fraud risk.
sched_r_related_corp_trust.section_512b_.subgroup_caveats: Health Care (E) and Housing & Shelter (L) dominate the per-filing-rate leaderboard; religion sits in the middle of the secular distribution.

sched_r_related_corp_trust.legal_domicil.what_it_is: US state or foreign country of the related corp/trust.
sched_r_related_corp_trust.legal_domicil.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Foreign for-profit subsidiaries of US 501(c)(3) filers warrant separate scrutiny under transfer-pricing (§482) and CFC rules.
sched_r_related_corp_trust.legal_domicil.what_a_high_rate_means: Concentrated foreign-domicile in related corps is rare in religion; uncommon in most secular sectors except International.
sched_r_related_corp_trust.legal_domicil.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: religion is overwhelmingly domestic; International (Q) and select Health Care orgs carry foreign exposure. Corp/trust domicile distribution by sector has not been tabulated here.

sched_r_transactions.transaction_amount.what_it_is: Dollar amount of the transaction with the related organization.
sched_r_transactions.transaction_amount.statutory_basis: Form 990 Schedule R Pt V; UBIT analysis under §512(b)(13) where the counterparty is a controlled entity.
sched_r_transactions.transaction_amount.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Where the money actually moves between affiliates. The diocesan-bankruptcy pattern (Milwaukee 2011, Davenport 2006, Tucson 2004) involves outsized pre-insolvency transfers from the diocese to related cemetery trusts and property-holding entities. Routine intercompany operating transfers in a health-system context look the same on the form but have different motive structures.
sched_r_transactions.transaction_amount.what_a_high_rate_means: High aggregate transfer amounts in a sector indicate intensive corporate-family use; not inherently fraud-adjacent.
sched_r_transactions.transaction_amount.what_a_low_rate_means: Standalone orgs without affiliates rarely populate Pt V.
sched_r_transactions.transaction_amount.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Per-filing Pt V disclosure rate: religion 5.20% (4,494 of 86,455 filings) ranks #21 of 24 majors. Health Care (E) leads at 26.52%, Housing & Shelter (L) 20.80%, Employment (J) 18.15%. Religion sits among the lowest sectors on Pt V density.
sched_r_transactions.transaction_amount.subgroup_caveats: Health Care (E), Housing & Shelter (L), Education (B 12.82%) have legitimate high-volume intercompany transfers.

sched_r_transactions.transaction_type_co.what_it_is: Single-letter code for transaction type (A through S). Decoded in the txn_type_codes block of codebook.json.
sched_r_transactions.transaction_type_co.statutory_basis: Form 990 Schedule R Pt V structured codes.
sched_r_transactions.transaction_type_co.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Codes are diagnostic: A (rent/royalty/annuity from related org) is the canonical §512(b)(13) UBIT trigger. D/E (loans) raise the same insider-lending concerns as Sched L Pt II but at the entity level. G/H/I (asset sale/purchase/exchange) are the pre-bankruptcy transfer pattern. R/S (other transfer) are the catch-all that often hides what doesn't fit elsewhere.
sched_r_transactions.transaction_type_co.what_a_high_rate_means: Concentration in codes G/H/I/R/S is more diagnostic than concentration in codes B/C (gift/grant) or N (shared facilities). Asset transfers warrant scrutiny; grants and shared facilities are typically benign.
sched_r_transactions.transaction_type_co.what_a_low_rate_means: Sectors with mostly B/C/N profiles have low intercompany-asset-flow concern.
sched_r_transactions.transaction_type_co.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: regulatory and ministry-finance framing predicts religion concentrates in codes B/C (grants between affiliated ministries) and N (shared facilities); secular Health Care concentrates in L/M/J/K (services and leases reflecting system operating models). Code distribution by sector has not been tabulated here.
sched_r_transactions.transaction_type_co.subgroup_caveats: Health Care and Education concentrate in L/M/J/K (operating system); Philanthropy (T) concentrates in B (grants to grantees) per regulatory framing.

sched_r_transactions.method_of_determini.what_it_is: How the org valued the transaction — FMV, cost, cash, arm's-length, invoice, etc.
sched_r_transactions.method_of_determini.statutory_basis: Reg. §53.4958-4(b) FMV standard; informally guides Pt V valuation.
sched_r_transactions.method_of_determini.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: 'FMV' and 'arm's-length' are the safe-harbor methods. 'Cost' on a related-party transaction is the gray-area method — cost-based pricing between affiliates is normal in shared-services contexts but does not establish arm's-length terms for FMV-sensitive transactions like rent or royalty. Blank or 'N/A' should not be tolerated by counsel; their presence indicates lax review.
sched_r_transactions.method_of_determini.what_a_high_rate_means: High 'FMV'/'arm's-length' rate is the healthy signal; high 'cost'/'cash' rate warrants follow-up.
sched_r_transactions.method_of_determini.what_a_low_rate_means: Not directly meaningful; read by method distribution rather than rate.
sched_r_transactions.method_of_determini.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis (not measured in this corpus): regulatory framing predicts smaller, less-counseled filers (including much of the religion corpus) lean toward 'cost'/'cash' framing while larger, more-counseled secular filers lean toward 'FMV'/'arm's-length.' Method-text distribution has not been mined in this corpus.
sched_r_transactions.method_of_determini.subgroup_caveats: Synonyms are canonicalized at data prep; underlying free text has dozens of variants.

sched_j_main.first_class_or_charter_trav.what_it_is: True = the org provides first-class or charter travel for officers/key employees.
sched_j_main.first_class_or_charter_trav.statutory_basis: Reg. §53.4958-4(c) treats personal-use airfare beyond reasonable business need as compensation; if not reported as such, it's excess benefit.
sched_j_main.first_class_or_charter_trav.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Specifically Grassley-flagged at Copeland (private jet) and Hinn ministries. First-class/charter is not per se improper but must be reported as compensation or justified as business necessity; the disclosure here is the structural admission, the test is whether the value is in W-2 box 1.
sched_j_main.first_class_or_charter_trav.what_a_high_rate_means: Sector-level concentration in luxury-perk disclosures correlates with founder-CEO governance.
sched_j_main.first_class_or_charter_trav.what_a_low_rate_means: Most filers do not provide first-class/charter; the field has low base rates across all sectors.
sched_j_main.first_class_or_charter_trav.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Per-filing rate by sector for this specific Sched J Pt I boolean is not separately tabulated in current rel_vs_sec.json (the Sched J Pt I leaderboard there counts 'any Sched J row' not 'first-class travel = True'). The Grassley-flagged broadcast-ministry pattern is established in regulatory record; sector-level magnitudes here are hypothesis.
sched_j_main.first_class_or_charter_trav.subgroup_caveats: Health Care (E) executive comp packages routinely include first-class as part of recruitment, per regulatory record.

sched_j_main.travel_companions.what_it_is: True = the org pays for travel companions (spouse/family) of officers.
sched_j_main.travel_companions.statutory_basis: Same §4958 framework as first_class — spousal travel is compensation unless business-necessary.
sched_j_main.travel_companions.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Grassley specifically named travel-companion payment as a category at multiple ministries. The disclosure is the structural admission; reasonableness depends on whether the companion serves a documented business function.
sched_j_main.travel_companions.what_a_high_rate_means: Higher rates in religion suggest spouse-as-co-pastor or spouse-as-ministry-partner patterns per regulatory framing.
sched_j_main.travel_companions.what_a_low_rate_means: Low base rate across all sectors.
sched_j_main.travel_companions.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: regulatory framing predicts religion runs higher than secular on travel-companion payments because of spouse-as-ministry-partner doctrine in evangelical and prosperity contexts. The specific per-filing rate for travel_companions=True by sector is not separately tabulated here.
sched_j_main.travel_companions.subgroup_caveats: Religion-specific phenomenon per regulatory record; minimal secular comparison value.

sched_j_main.tax_indemnification.what_it_is: True = the org provides tax gross-up payments (org pays the officer's tax bill on certain benefits).
sched_j_main.tax_indemnification.statutory_basis: Gross-up payments are themselves compensation under Reg. §1.61-21; treatment under §4958 turns on whether they're documented in initial comp approval.
sched_j_main.tax_indemnification.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Grassley-flagged at multiple ministries. A gross-up that isn't in the comp committee's contemporaneous documentation defeats the rebuttable presumption.
sched_j_main.tax_indemnification.what_a_high_rate_means: Higher rates indicate sophisticated executive-comp packaging.
sched_j_main.tax_indemnification.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: Health Care and Education lead secular on this perk per regulatory framing; religion is mid-pack overall but elevated in the broadcasting-ministry subset. Sector-specific gross-up rate has not been tabulated here.
sched_j_main.tax_indemnification.subgroup_caveats: Sector size correlates with sophistication; control for org size.

sched_j_main.discretionary_spending_acco.what_it_is: True = officers have a discretionary spending account.
sched_j_main.discretionary_spending_acco.statutory_basis: Accountable-plan rules under Reg. §1.62-2; non-accountable plans are taxable to the employee.
sched_j_main.discretionary_spending_acco.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Discretionary spending accounts without strict accountable-plan procedures are the canonical mechanism for unrestricted insider expense flows. The Grassley inquiry traced credit-card-as-discretionary-account patterns at several ministries.
sched_j_main.discretionary_spending_acco.what_a_high_rate_means: Concentration of discretionary accounts warrants scrutiny of the accountable-plan documentation — not visible on the 990 itself.
sched_j_main.discretionary_spending_acco.what_a_low_rate_means: Most orgs use accountable-plan reimbursement, not discretionary accounts.
sched_j_main.discretionary_spending_acco.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Both corpora are low single-digit rates per regulatory framing; not a top-tier comparison metric. Per-filing rate for this specific boolean has not been separately tabulated.
sched_j_main.discretionary_spending_acco.subgroup_caveats: Cell sizes small; statistical noise dominates sector-level differences.

sched_j_main.housing_allowance_residence.what_it_is: True = the org provides a housing allowance or residence for personal use.
sched_j_main.housing_allowance_residence.statutory_basis: IRC §107 minister housing-allowance exclusion (constitutionally challenged in FFRF v. Lew, FFRF v. Werfel; partially upheld); for non-ministers, §119 convenience-of-employer test.
sched_j_main.housing_allowance_residence.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: For ordained ministers, §107 allows a designated housing allowance to be excluded from gross income up to FMV. The compliance question is whether the designated amount actually equals fair-rental-value of the parsonage — over-designation is excess benefit. For non-ministers, housing is straight compensation unless §119 applies.
sched_j_main.housing_allowance_residence.what_a_high_rate_means: Religion-corpus rate is structurally elevated because §107 applies. High rates in secular sectors typically reflect campus-housing programs (Education) or live-on-site requirements (Housing & Shelter).
sched_j_main.housing_allowance_residence.what_a_low_rate_means: Most secular orgs don't provide housing; absence is the baseline.
sched_j_main.housing_allowance_residence.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: This is the field where the comparison is most apples-to-oranges. Religion's elevated rate reflects §107's specific carve-out, not a behavioral difference. The fraud question within religion is FMV-comparability of designated allowance, not the rate of disclosure. Per-filing rate for this specific Sched J Pt I boolean has not been tabulated separately from the overall Sched J Pt I 'any row' rate.
sched_j_main.housing_allowance_residence.subgroup_caveats: Treat religion separately on this field; secular-vs-secular comparison is the more meaningful axis.

sched_j_main.personal_services.what_it_is: True = the org pays for personal services for officers (household staff, personal assistants for non-business work).
sched_j_main.personal_services.statutory_basis: Personal-services payments are straight compensation under Reg. §1.61-21 and §4958-4(c).
sched_j_main.personal_services.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Grassley-flagged. Personal-service payments are nearly always compensation; the disclosure question is whether they're reported as such on the W-2 or treated as 'org expenses.'
sched_j_main.personal_services.what_a_high_rate_means: Concentration here is consistent with founder-CEO household-as-org-cost patterns.
sched_j_main.personal_services.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Both corpora have very low rates per regulatory framing; not a high-volume comparison metric. Per-filing rate not separately tabulated here.
sched_j_main.personal_services.subgroup_caveats: Cell sizes small; rare positives are individually diagnostic.

sched_j_main.health_or_social_club_dues.what_it_is: True = the org pays health-club or social-club dues for officers.
sched_j_main.health_or_social_club_dues.statutory_basis: Club dues are nondeductible business expenses under IRC §274(a)(3); when paid for officers, they are compensation.
sched_j_main.health_or_social_club_dues.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Grassley-flagged. Club dues are universally compensation; the disclosure question is W-2 reporting.
sched_j_main.health_or_social_club_dues.what_a_high_rate_means: Concentration indicates loose-perk culture more than fraud per se.
sched_j_main.health_or_social_club_dues.what_a_low_rate_means: Most orgs don't pay club dues.
sched_j_main.health_or_social_club_dues.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: secular Health Care and Education run somewhat higher than religion per regulatory framing. Per-filing rate by sector not separately tabulated here.
sched_j_main.health_or_social_club_dues.subgroup_caveats: Sector-specific perk culture, not necessarily fraud signal.

sched_j_main.written_policy_for_above.what_it_is: True = there is a written policy covering the above perks.
sched_j_main.written_policy_for_above.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Empty_in_corpus in this dataset; analytical axis unavailable.

sched_j_main.compensation_committee.what_it_is: True = a compensation committee sets officer comp.
sched_j_main.compensation_committee.statutory_basis: Reg. §53.4958-6(c)(1) — independent body is the first prerequisite for the rebuttable presumption.
sched_j_main.compensation_committee.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Absence of a comp committee is the most basic governance deficiency for setting officer comp. Without an independent body, the rebuttable presumption is unavailable.
sched_j_main.compensation_committee.what_a_high_rate_means: Higher rates indicate professionalized comp governance.
sched_j_main.compensation_committee.what_a_low_rate_means: Sectors without comp committees rely on whole-board or unilateral comp-setting; weaker procedural defense in §4958 challenges.
sched_j_main.compensation_committee.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: religion has lower comp-committee rates than secular — smaller boards, less specialization. Religion's per-filing 'any Sched J Pt I row' rate is 9.23% (ranks #24 of 24 majors), below every secular sector; this is the closest available proxy in current data, but the specific compensation_committee=True rate by sector is not separately tabulated.
sched_j_main.compensation_committee.subgroup_caveats: Org size correlates with comp-committee presence; control for size before reading as religion-specific finding.

sched_j_main.independent_compensation_co.what_it_is: True = an independent compensation consultant was used.
sched_j_main.independent_compensation_co.statutory_basis: Reg. §53.4958-6(c)(2)(ii)(B) — reliance on appropriate data, including outside consultant, is the second presumption prerequisite.
sched_j_main.independent_compensation_co.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Empty_in_corpus in this dataset; analytical axis unavailable.

sched_j_main.compensation_survey.what_it_is: True = a compensation survey was used.
sched_j_main.compensation_survey.statutory_basis: Reg. §53.4958-6(c)(2)(i) — comparability data from independent compensation surveys is the second prerequisite for the rebuttable presumption.
sched_j_main.compensation_survey.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Absence of survey-based comparability data leaves the org without a documented basis for asserting comp reasonableness, defeating the rebuttable presumption.
sched_j_main.compensation_survey.what_a_high_rate_means: Higher rates indicate the org is positioning itself for rebuttable-presumption defense.
sched_j_main.compensation_survey.what_a_low_rate_means: Sectors without survey reliance are exposed in any §4958 challenge.
sched_j_main.compensation_survey.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: religion lags secular substantially on survey use; religious orgs cite the difficulty of finding 'comparable' ministry executives. Per-filing rate for this specific boolean by sector is not separately tabulated.
sched_j_main.compensation_survey.subgroup_caveats: Sector size correlates with survey use.

sched_j_main.approval_by_board_or_comp_c.what_it_is: True = comp was approved by the board or the comp committee.
sched_j_main.approval_by_board_or_comp_c.statutory_basis: Reg. §53.4958-6(c)(3) — contemporaneous documentation of approval is the third prerequisite.
sched_j_main.approval_by_board_or_comp_c.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Empty_in_corpus in this dataset; analytical axis unavailable.

sched_j_main.severance_payment.what_it_is: True = the org paid severance to a former officer.
sched_j_main.severance_payment.statutory_basis: Severance is compensation under §4958-4 unless characterized as separation from contract; large-dollar severance to disqualified persons is the golden-parachute risk.
sched_j_main.severance_payment.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Severance that wasn't pre-approved with comparability documentation is excess-benefit-eligible. The largest §4958 cases in the IRS exam history (cf. Sta-Home Health Agency, Caracci v. Comm'r) involved severance/buyout payments characterized as excess benefits.
sched_j_main.severance_payment.what_a_high_rate_means: Health-care-system executive turnover drives high secular rates here. Religion-corpus rates are lower and concentrated in larger ministries.
sched_j_main.severance_payment.what_a_low_rate_means: Smaller orgs don't pay severance; absence is the baseline.
sched_j_main.severance_payment.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: secular substantially higher across the board; reflects executive labor-market structure, not necessarily compliance posture. Per-filing severance-payment rate by sector not separately tabulated here.
sched_j_main.severance_payment.subgroup_caveats: Health Care (E), Education (B), Housing (L) lead per regulatory framing; sector-structural.

sched_j_main.supplemental_nonqualified_r.what_it_is: True = the org has a supplemental non-qualified retirement plan (SERP) for officers.
sched_j_main.supplemental_nonqualified_r.statutory_basis: IRC §457(b)/(f) governs nonqualified deferred comp for tax-exempts; §4958-4 applies for reasonableness.
sched_j_main.supplemental_nonqualified_r.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: SERPs are legal but high-stakes — the accumulated deferred amount can become a substantial excess-benefit exposure if not documented contemporaneously. The Caracci-line cases include SERP-equivalent arrangements characterized as excess benefits.
sched_j_main.supplemental_nonqualified_r.what_a_high_rate_means: SERP use is institutionally sophisticated; concentrated in larger orgs.
sched_j_main.supplemental_nonqualified_r.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: secular substantially higher; religion has lower base rates because religious orgs are smaller on average and use §403(b) instead of SERPs. Per-filing SERP rate by sector not separately tabulated here.
sched_j_main.supplemental_nonqualified_r.subgroup_caveats: Health Care (E), Education (B) dominate per regulatory framing.

sched_j_main.equity_based_compensation.statutory_basis: Tax-exempts cannot issue stock; equity-based comp typically means phantom stock, SAR, or partnership-interest grants tied to related taxable entities.
sched_j_main.equity_based_compensation.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Equity-based comp at a 501(c)(3) is unusual and signals an intricate related-entity structure where the officer holds an interest in a controlled for-profit subsidiary. Inurement risk is high.
sched_j_main.equity_based_compensation.what_a_high_rate_means: Rare and worth investigating wherever present.
sched_j_main.equity_based_compensation.what_a_low_rate_means: Most 501(c)(3)s do not use equity-based comp.
sched_j_main.equity_based_compensation.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: both corpora carry very low base rates; secular Health Care has some real positives tied to physician-practice equity. Per-filing equity-comp rate by sector not separately tabulated here.
sched_j_main.equity_based_compensation.subgroup_caveats: Health Care (E), Science & Tech (U) are the structural exceptions.

sched_j_main.compensation_contingent_on_.what_it_is: True = officer comp is tied to org revenues.
sched_j_main.compensation_contingent_on_.statutory_basis: Reg. §1.501(c)(3)-1(c)(2) inurement; Rev. Rul. 69-383; GCM 39862 — revenue-contingent comp is presumptive private inurement unless strictly cabined.
sched_j_main.compensation_contingent_on_.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Revenue-contingent comp creates the precise alignment of interest that the inurement doctrine prohibits. Where present, the org should have ironclad documentation showing the formula is reasonable, the cap is meaningful, and the arrangement was approved with comparability data.
sched_j_main.compensation_contingent_on_.what_a_high_rate_means: Sectors with elevated rates are operating at the edge of the inurement doctrine.
sched_j_main.compensation_contingent_on_.what_a_low_rate_means: Most orgs avoid this structure entirely because of the inurement risk.
sched_j_main.compensation_contingent_on_.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Per-filing 'contingent comp' rate (any sched_j_main row with revenues OR net-earnings contingent = True): religion 0.0625% (54 of 86,455), secular 0.491% (5,694 of 1,160,678). Ratio 0.13× — secular is ~7.9× religion. The biggest comparison gap in the dataset in the direction OPPOSITE to §4958. Counter-intuitive only until you note that religious orgs operate under direct theological-doctrine constraints against revenue-tied pay (multiple denominations explicitly bar it), while secular nonprofits (especially Health Care and Education) treat productivity-bonus arrangements as standard executive comp.
sched_j_main.compensation_contingent_on_.subgroup_caveats: Health Care (E) leads secular sectors because physician-productivity-based pay is sector-standard. Read the secular figure with sector decomposition.

sched_j_main.compensation_contingent_on_.what_it_is: True = officer comp is tied to org net earnings.
sched_j_main.compensation_contingent_on_.statutory_basis: Same inurement framework; net-earnings-contingent is even more directly the inurement prohibition's target (Reg. §1.501(c)(3)-1(c)(2)'s 'no part of net earnings' language).
sched_j_main.compensation_contingent_on_.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Net-earnings-contingent comp is the most direct possible form of inurement. The statutory text literally prohibits 'inurement of net earnings' to private individuals; this disclosure is the org admitting it has structured comp in exactly that form.
sched_j_main.compensation_contingent_on_.what_a_high_rate_means: Any non-trivial rate is concerning at the field level; a sector with elevated rates is operating at high inurement-doctrine exposure.
sched_j_main.compensation_contingent_on_.what_a_low_rate_means: Most orgs do not have this; absence is the baseline.
sched_j_main.compensation_contingent_on_.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Same direction as revenue-contingent (subsumed into the combined contingent-comp metric in rel_vs_sec.json): secular is materially higher than religion. See sched_j_main.compensation_contingent_on_revenues for the combined 0.0625% vs 0.491% comparison.

sched_j_main.non_fixed_payments.what_it_is: True = the org made bonus or discretionary payments without a fixed written formula.
sched_j_main.non_fixed_payments.statutory_basis: Reg. §53.4958-4(b)(1)(ii)(B) — non-fixed payments without contemporaneous approval and documentation defeat the rebuttable presumption.
sched_j_main.non_fixed_payments.why_it_signals_fraud_or_misappropriation: Discretionary bonuses without written formula are not per se improper but require contemporaneous board approval to qualify for the rebuttable presumption. Without that approval they are excess-benefit-eligible.
sched_j_main.non_fixed_payments.what_a_high_rate_means: Sectors with high rates have weaker structural protection against §4958 challenges.
sched_j_main.non_fixed_payments.how_to_compare_religion_vs_secular: Hypothesis: secular rates somewhat higher; non-fixed bonus is a more common feature of professionalized executive comp. Per-filing non-fixed-payment rate by sector not separately tabulated here.
sched_j_main.non_fixed_payments.subgroup_caveats: Health Care, Education lead per regulatory framing.

sched_j_compensation.base_compensation_f.what_it_is: Base salary paid by the filing org.
sched_j_compensation.base_compensation_f.statutory_basis: W-2 box 1 reportable comp; basis for FMV analysis under Reg. §53.4958-4.
